results.title: Open-Set 3D object detection in LiDAR data as an Out-of-Distribution problem
results.content: Our work redefines the open-set 3D Object Detection problem in LiDAR data as an Out-Of-Distribution (OOD) problem to detect outlier objects. We establish a comparative benchmark and show that two-stage OOD methods, notably autolabelling, show promising results for 3D OOD Object Detection. Our contributions include setting a rigorous evaluation protocol by examining the evaluation of hyperparameters and evaluating strategies for generating additional data to train an OOD-aware 3D object detector. In this paper, we redefine the open-set 3D Object Detection problem in LiDAR data as an Out-Of-Distribution (OOD) problem, setting a rigorous evaluation protocol by examining evaluation hyperparameters. Additionally, we evaluate methods for generating additional data to train an OOD-aware 3D object detector. Evaluating generation methods of additional data for training an OOD-aware 3D object detector. Furthermore, their resizing unknown generation method produces lesser results than top-K labelling, suggesting that using pseudo-labels from real OOD data can lead to better performance than reshaping known objects. ### III-A Viewing open-set 3D object detection as an OOD problem. We can view the Open Set detection as an out-of-distribution (OOD) prediction challenge, where our focus is on evaluating a base detector’s predictions and determining which of these correspond to genuine unknown objects in the scene. In our evaluation, we use metrics commonly employed in OOD detection, including AUROC, FPR-95, AUPR-E (with open classes as positives), and AUPR-S (with known classes as positives), to assess the model’s ability to distinguish between known and unknown objects. In our evaluation of OOD detection for 3D object detection, we selected several single-stage methods to ensure a comprehensive assessment, i.e. methods that directly use the output logits of the detection model. We then trained our MLP to detect OOD objects, using different generation methods of unknown objects, which we use as our ground truth. We illustrate these different generation methods in Figure 3 and compare these various representations of OOD objects and their impact on the training and performance of our additional module on real validation OOD data. Our work redefines the open-set 3D Object Detection problem in LiDAR data as an Out-Of-Distribution problem. Additionally, we show that two-stage methods show promise for OOD 3D Object Detection and underline the potential of autolabelling methods.
